cards.title: Fewest bike trips
cards.prompt: A courier bike can carry at most two packages per trip, and their combined weight can't go over a limit W. Given the package weights, what's the fewest trips needed to deliver all of them?
brief_lines: At most two packages per trip
Combined weight per trip at most W
facts_if_asked: Every single package weighs at most W.
Weights are positive integers.
Up to one hundred thousand packages.
Example: weights 3, 2, 2, 1 with W of 3 needs three trips.
The input list may be reordered.
follow_ups: Why does pairing the heaviest with the lightest work?
What's the time and space cost?
What if every package is heavier than half of W?
cards.twist: Now the bike can carry up to three packages per trip, same weight limit. What changes, and why is it harder?
hints: What are you weighing right now?
Which package is hardest to place, and who could it share a trip with?
What if the packages were sorted by weight?
Try pairing the heaviest remaining package with the lightest remaining one, if they fit together.
strong_answer_covers: Clarifies that no single package is over W
Sorts, then two pointers pairing heaviest with lightest
O of n log n time, constant extra space beyond the sort
A short exchange argument for why the pairing is safe
Tests: all heavy, all light, a single package, exact fits at W
Twist: sees it is a bin packing style problem, offers a reasonable heuristic and says it may not be optimal
Does not claim the three per trip version stays greedy optimal without an argument

cards.title: Repeat message filter
cards.prompt: A service sends you log lines, each with a timestamp in seconds and a message. Print a message only if the same text wasn't printed in the last ten seconds. Write the function that decides whether to print.
brief_lines: Input: timestamp in seconds, message text
Print unless the same text printed in the last 10 seconds
Return true to print, false to drop
facts_if_asked: Timestamps arrive in non decreasing order.
A message printed at second 1 may print again at second 11, not at second 10.
Messages are short strings, compared exactly.
Many different messages, millions per day.
follow_ups: Memory grows forever. How would you bound it?
What if timestamps can arrive slightly out of order?
cards.twist: Now many threads call this at once. What breaks, and how would you fix it?
hints: Talk me through what you need to remember between calls.
What do you need to look up when a message arrives?
Is there a structure that gives you constant time lookup by text?
What if you kept a map from message text to the last time you printed it?
strong_answer_covers: Map from message text to last printed time
Constant time per call
Updates the time only when it prints
Bounds memory with a queue of time and text, or periodic cleanup of entries older than ten seconds
Concurrency: a lock, or sharding the map by a hash of the message
Tests: exactly ten seconds apart, nine seconds apart, interleaved messages
Notices that updating the time on dropped messages changes behaviour

cards.title: Longest calm stretch
cards.prompt: You have daily sensor readings as a list of numbers. Find the length of the longest run of consecutive days where the highest and lowest reading in that run differ by at most K.
brief_lines: Daily readings, a list of numbers
Max minus min in the run at most K
facts_if_asked: Up to one hundred thousand readings.
Readings are integers, can be negative.
K is zero or more.
Example: readings 8, 2, 4, 7 with K of 4 gives 2, from 2 and 4.
An empty list returns 0.
follow_ups: Why does each index enter and leave the window at most once?
How do you know the current max and min quickly?
cards.twist: Now the readings arrive as a stream and you must report the best length so far after each reading. What changes?
hints: What are you weighing right now?
If a window is valid, what happens when you extend it by one day?
Can you keep the window's max and min without rescanning it?
What if you kept two deques of indices, one with decreasing values for the max and one increasing for the min?
strong_answer_covers: Brute force is quadratic or worse and says why
Sliding window with two pointers
Max and min via two monotonic deques for linear time, or a sorted structure for n log n
Argues each index is added and removed once
Tests: K of zero, all equal, strictly increasing, a single reading
Stream twist: same window works online, best so far is a running max
Does not call a window rescan linear

cards.title: Course module order
cards.prompt: An online course has modules numbered zero to n minus one. Some modules must be finished before others unlock, given as pairs: before, after. Return an order to take every module that respects all of these, or say it's impossible.
brief_lines: Return a valid order, or none if impossible
facts_if_asked: Up to ten thousand modules and fifty thousand pairs.
Any valid order is fine.
Pairs never repeat.
A module that depends on itself makes it impossible.
Example: n of 3, pairs 0 before 1 and 1 before 2 gives 0, 1, 2.
follow_ups: How do you detect that it's impossible?
Could you tell the learner which modules form the loop?
cards.twist: Modules with no dependency between them can be taken in the same term. What's the fewest terms needed?
hints: Talk me through how you'd model the modules and pairs.
Which modules can you take right now, at the very start?
What happens to the other modules when you finish one?
What if you kept a count of unmet prerequisites per module and a queue of modules whose count is zero?
strong_answer_covers: Models it as a directed graph
Kahn's algorithm with in-degree counts, or DFS with three colours
Impossible exactly when not every module gets placed, meaning a cycle
Linear in modules plus pairs
Finding the loop: DFS with the recursion stack, or the leftover nodes
Twist: process the queue level by level; the number of levels is the fewest terms
Asks whether a cycle can happen instead of assuming it cannot

cards.title: Search suggestions
cards.prompt: A shop has a list of product names. As a user types a search word one letter at a time, after each letter show up to three products that start with what's typed so far, alphabetically first. Return the suggestions for every letter.
brief_lines: User types a word letter by letter
After each letter: up to 3 matches by prefix
facts_if_asked: Names are lowercase letters only.
Up to ten thousand products, names up to thirty letters.
If nothing matches, return an empty list for that letter.
Example: products bag, bat, bath, cat; typing ba gives bag, bat, bath after both letters.
follow_ups: What if there are a million products and many users typing at once?
Where would you do the sorting?
cards.twist: Now rank suggestions by popularity instead of alphabetically. What do you store differently?
hints: What are you weighing right now?
If the list were sorted, where would the matches for a prefix sit?
How can you jump to the first name that is at least the prefix?
What if you sorted once, then binary searched for the prefix after each letter and took the next three names?
strong_answer_covers: Sort once up front
Binary search for the first name at least the prefix, then check up to three
Per keystroke cost log n plus a small constant
Alternative: a trie with the top three stored at each node; trades memory for query time
Tests: no matches, fewer than three matches, a product equal to the prefix
Twist: store top three by popularity per trie node, update on popularity changes

reference_solution.time: O(n log n) to sort, then O(log n) per letter

lines.text: result.append([p for p in products[i:i + 3] if p.startswith(prefix)])
